newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary needs structural reforms-EU-Hungary report.
newsitem.headline: Hungary needs structural reforms-EU-Hungary report.

text.p: Hungary needs further deep structural reforms to improve the balance of its budget and reduce domestic state debt, a joint report of the Finance Ministry and the European Union (EU) said on Wednesday.
The European Union and the Finance Ministry of Hungary, which hopes to join the (EU) around 2000, evaluated the government's five-year economic plan in the joint report.
The report said that Hungary needed to streamline the public sector and introduce comprehensive reforms in the pension, the health care and the tax systems.
Improvements in the central state budget in 1996 compensated for a rise in the social security's deficit to levels four times above the target, it said.

But the government delayed earnings tax refunds and certain government investments until this year, and the introduction of the new pension system planned for 1998 will increase the government budget deficit for the short term, the report added.

The government should discourage tax evasion by further widening the circle of taxed incomes and lowering tax and social security contribution rates, improving the effectiveness of the economy, the report said.
Inflation, which is seen in the government strategy being cut to between four and five percent by 2002 from 17 to 19 percent forecast for 1997, should be brought down without substantial jumps.

The report said that a stable trend in the decline in inflation, legislation to make the collection of claims less risky and the launch of pension funds from 1998 should help companies, to which banks offer only short-term funding, to get to longer-term loans.
According to the five-year plan, Hungary projects increasing gross domestic product (GDP) growth rates of two to five percent for the period between 1997 and 2002.
The government budget deficit is seen dropping to between three and 3.5 percent of the GDP from a five percent forecast from this year.
The current account deficit is expected to stabilise at $2.5 billion by 2000, down from the 1997 target of $2 billion.

The report expects exports to continue to rise sharply, tourism to maintain last year's high level of revenues generation, and Hungary's gross foreign debt and external debt service to decrease in the next five years.
The government strategy forecasts annual foreign direct investment inflows of $1.5 to $2 billion also for the next five years.
